entries.note: From Greek [[from:mathema]], science or knowledge, a general word for learning until [[see:Pythagoras]] applied it to arithmetic and geometry; Americans abbreviate it [[see:math]], Brits [[see:maths]].
The American abbreviation of [[from:mathematics]], which Jess defends as logical because abbreviations like econ aren't pluralised; Brits find it irritating.
The British abbreviation of [[from:mathematics]], kept plural because the full word is; Brits often correct anyone saying [[see:math]].
The Greek of theorem fame who applied the Greek word behind [[see:mathematics]] specifically to arithmetic and geometry.
Someone learned in many different things, not just mathematical sciences; its second half shares the root of [[same-root:mathematics]].
Its math is an Old English word for a mowing or cutting of grass, unrelated to [[unrelated:mathematics]]; it suggests things cut down by disaster or war.
From Arabic [[from:al-jabr]], reunion of broken parts or restoration, also used for bone-setting, via the book by [[see:al-Khwarizmi]].
Persian mathematician who wrote the book behind [[see:algebra]] in Baghdad around 820; his name means 'from Khwarezm', like da Vinci, and gave [[gave:algorithm]].

entries.term: The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing
entries.note: [[see:al-Khwarizmi]]'s book, written in Baghdad around 820, whose title is translated variously and which gave us [[gave:algebra]].
The variety spoken in Morocco, where Jess studied: fundamentally Arabic but a blend of several languages, heavily influenced by French.
A corruption of the name of [[from:al-Khwarizmi]], which means 'the one from Khwarezm'.
Compared with [[see:al-Khwarizmi]]: calling him da Vinci just means 'from Vinci', so he should really be called Leonardo.
The place [[see:al-Khwarizmi]]'s name refers to, in modern-day Uzbekistan.
From Arabic [[from:sifr]], zero or empty, via Latin [[from:zephirum]]; positional systems of the Babylonians, Maya and Gupta India gave it its senses; Romans lacked it.
Also from Arabic [[from:sifr]], closer to the original; besides a code, in 14th-century English it meant the symbol for [[same-root:zero]].
From Old English [[from:hund]] plus a suffix meaning 'a count of'; shares a root with [[same-root:centum]] and [[same-root:hekaton]], and in Old English meant 120.
Latin for a hundred, sharing a root with [[same-root:hundred]] through regular sound swaps of C to H and T to D.
Greek for a hundred, related to [[same-root:hundred]].
A hundred meaning 120, or six score, reflecting Germanic counting where the first twelve numbers mattered; contrasted with the [[see:short hundred]].
A hundred meaning 100, as opposed to the [[see:long hundred]] of 120.
Literally a 'swollen hundred': the ending is probably related to [[same-root:hundred]], the start to an ancient root meaning strong or swollen; originally just a big number.
The Roman word for a big number, vaguer than exactly ten hundred, like early [[see:thousand]].
A big thousand, its ending a Latin intensifier.
One followed by nine zeros on the [[see:long scale]], still used in most European languages; Britain dropped it for the American [[see:billion]]; ends in intensifying [[see:-ard]].
The American system, adopted by Britain, where a [[see:billion]] is one followed by nine zeros.
The older British and European system alternating -illion and -illiard, so a [[see:billion]] is a million million and nine zeros is a [[see:milliard]].
The British billion was one followed by twelve zeros until Britain adopted the American nine-zero billion, largely due to the dollar's power.
An American trillion equals the British [[see:billion]] on the [[see:long scale]].
An American quadrillion equals a British [[see:billiard]].
On the [[see:long scale]], the number after the British [[see:billion]], equal to an American [[see:quadrillion]].
On the [[see:long scale]], the number following the British trillion.
An intensifying suffix found in [[see:milliard]], [[see:drunkard]], [[see:dotard]], [[see:wizard]] and [[see:bastard]].
An example of the intensifying [[see:-ard]] suffix.
An example of the intensifying [[see:-ard]] suffix.
An example of the intensifying [[see:-ard]] suffix.
An example of the intensifying [[see:-ard]] suffix.
Debated as adjective versus noun; to the ancient Greeks a myriad was specifically 10,000; unlike [[see:milliard]] despite the similar sound.
Indian English for 100,000, from Hindi and originally Sanskrit, needed because Indian numbering puts commas every two digits.
Indian English for ten million, used alongside [[see:lakh]] because of the Indian comma-every-two-digits convention.
One followed by 100 zeros, coined by nine-year-old [[see:Milton Sirotta]], nephew of [[see:Edward Kasner]]; the search engine [[gave:Google]] is named after it.
The search engine, named after the number [[from:googol]] but spelled differently.
The nine-year-old who coined [[see:googol]] while walking with his uncle in the New Jersey Palisades.
Mathematician who asked his nephew [[see:Milton Sirotta]] for a name for one followed by 100 zeros, getting [[see:googol]].
Ten to the power of a [[from:googol]], not just another hundred zeros; 'plex' means 'to the power of'.
Ten to the power of a [[from:googolplex]], an unimaginably big number that exists as a word but has no practical use.
The word for base-20 counting; its start relates to French [[from:vingt]], twenty, and it is formed like [[see:decimal]].
[[see:vigesimal]] is formed the same way.
Latin for a pebble, also a kidney or bladder stone; diminutive of [[from:calx]], chalk or limestone; named after pebbles used for counting.
Latin for chalk or limestone, which gave [[gave:calculus]] and is related to German [[same-root:Kalk]].
German for the [[equivalent:limescale]] in kettles, which Rob battles in hard-water Berlin; related to [[same-root:calx]]; French says [[equivalent:calcaire]].
The British word for the buildup German calls [[equivalent:Kalk]]; Jess would say calcium buildup.
French for kettle [[equivalent:limescale]].
Related to [[same-root:calculus]], like calculate, both about counting with little pebbles.
German for calculator, related to English [[same-root:reckon]].
Means to calculate, as in [[see:after the feast the reckoning]]; related to German [[same-root:Rechner]], [[same-root:Rechnung]] and [[same-root:reckless]].
Quoted to show the calculating sense of [[see:reckon]].
German for a bill, literally the reckoning, from the same root as [[same-root:reckon]].
Without calculating consequences, from the same root as [[same-root:reckon]]; an [[see:orphan negative]], since nobody is reckful.
A negative word without a positive counterpart, like [[see:reckless]] with no reckful.
Literally earth measurement, one of the oldest forms of maths, needed for land, boundaries and taxes, later developed by [[see:Euclid]].
The study of the earth, compared with [[same-root:geometry]].
Literally writing or drawing about the earth, compared with [[same-root:geometry]].
Took [[see:geometry]] into a modern mathematical system.
Preferred by both hosts because it is based on an estimated measurement of the Earth, so centimetres add up to a round number around the world.
The quaint unit Rob used to ask for when buying sweets as a child, before grams.
Jess still buys milk in quarts; four make a gallon, one of the old-fashioned American measures.
Contains the same measurement element as [[same-root:geometry]].
A measurement around something, sharing the measurement element of [[same-root:geometry]].
Literally triangle measurement, sharing the measurement element of [[same-root:geometry]].
From Greek [[from:arithmos]], number or counting, not the measurement root, though sometimes thought so, giving forms based on [[see:ars metrica]].
Medieval Latin phrase that [[see:arithmetic]] was wrongly thought to come from, producing spellings in medieval mathematical writing.
British phrase for reading, writing and [[see:arithmetic]], though only one of them begins with R.
Literally broken numbers, related to [[same-root:fracture]], [[same-root:fragile]] and [[same-root:fragment]].
Related to [[same-root:fraction]].
Related to [[same-root:fraction]].
Related to [[same-root:fraction]].
The noble title originally meant a companion or attendant, later a governor; from roots meaning 'with' and 'to go', unrelated to counting numbers.
From Old French [[from:conter]], also 'tell a story', from Latin [[from:computare]], to reckon together; unrelated to the noble title.
Means to tell a tale because the Old French counting word also meant telling a story, summing up an experience.
Like computing, from Latin [[from:computare]], to reckon together; French deliberately avoids it, saying [[equivalent:ordinateur]].
The French word chosen deliberately instead of [[equivalent:computer]], semantically similar: something that calculates or carries out an action.
The grocery counter is related to counting, as a place where counting happens.
The infinity sign, from Latin [[from:lemniscatus]], decorated with ribbons, and Greek [[from:lemniskos]]; [[see:James Booth]] adopted it for the symbol in 1811.
Mathematician and clergyman who in 1811 adopted [[see:lemniscate]] for the ribbon-like symbol in algebraic geometry.
